Aaron Copland, the Dean of American Composers, was born in 1900 and died in 1990. He crafted a distinctively American populist musical style, characterized by open harmonies that reflected the vast American landscape, and he integrated traditional folk tunes throughout his work. After early experiments in jazz and modernism, Copland shifted during the Great Depression and World War II to write accessible, patriotic music.

Appalachian Spring, completed in 1944, is his most famous ballet. Martha Graham commissioned and choreographed it, and it depicts a wedding celebration of a young pioneer couple in Pennsylvania. The work is most famous for incorporating the Shaker hymn Simple Gifts. Fanfare for the Common Man, written in 1942, is a brief, stirring work for brass and percussion composed during World War II, inspired by Vice President Henry A. Wallace's speech declaring the start of the Century of the Common Man. Rodeo, also from 1942, is a cowboy ballet choreographed by Agnes de Mille about a tomboy cowgirl seeking love on a ranch. Its most energetic movement is the famous Hoedown. Lincoln Portrait, completed in 1942, is a patriotic symphonic work featuring a speaker reciting passages from Abraham Lincoln's speeches and letters over an orchestral score that incorporates folk tunes like Camptown Races. His first cowboy ballet, Billy the Kid from 1938, depicts the life of the outlaw William Bonney and quotes traditional Western songs like Goodbye Old Paint.

Copland studied under Nadia Boulanger, the legendary French pedagogue in Paris, who went on to teach many of the leading American composers of the twentieth century. He was the central architect of the mid-twentieth-century American symphonic sound, collaborating with leading modern choreographers to create a distinct American ballet tradition, and he designed his open fourth and fifth intervals to evoke the sparse, expansive horizons of the American West.
